clue.text: Eccentric upset, coming round with letter

indicators.note: coming round means encircling, so one piece wraps itself around another
to upset something is to tip it over, so the word is turned upside down in this down clue

parts.note: droll means oddly amusing, whimsical
and is a synonym of with, joining two things

explanation.surface: Someone peculiar gets agitated when they come round carrying a letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' looks like something posted, but it means one who lets property; the wordplay builds the first half of LANDLORD inside the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A landlord lets out rooms or houses to tenants, so in the crossword sense he is a letter.

clue.text: Zealot contributing to upturn in pureness evidently

indicators.note: an upturn flips something over, so in a down clue the letters read from the bottom up
something contributing to a phrase is one part of it, so the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A religious fanatic's hand in a moral revival is plain to see in his purity.
explanation.walkthrough: The string ENESSE spans 'purENESS Evidently'; read upwards it becomes ESSENE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Essenes were an ascetic Jewish sect of the Second Temple period, devout to the point of fanaticism, so a member fits zealot.

clue.text: Soldier and sailor of renown producing magical plant?

parts.note: a man is a private soldier, as in officers and men
Sir Francis Drake, the Elizabethan seafarer

explanation.surface: A famous soldier and admiral team up and somehow produce an enchanted plant.
explanation.walkthrough: Drake is the English captain who sailed round the world and fought the Armada. The question mark admits the plant is only magical in folklore.
explanation.definitionFit: Mandrake root was credited in legend with powers, shrieking when pulled from the ground, so it is the classic plant of witchcraft.

clue.text: Big fight, not initially crazy, about artist

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece is placed around another
not initially means without the start, so the opening letter is removed

parts.note: daffy is informal for silly or mad
RA is a Royal Academician, the standard abbreviation for an artist

explanation.surface: A brawl that was not at first insane breaks out around a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: RA, for Royal Academician, is the stock crossword artist. 'Big fight' is fair because an affray is more than a scuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: An affray is a public brawl or disturbance, and in law a fight serious enough to frighten bystanders.

clue.text: French cathedral good — go there

parts.note: beau is French for fine or good-looking
je vais is French for I go

explanation.surface: A tourist tip: this French cathedral is fine, so go and see it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'There' means in France, so the words for good and go are taken in French.
explanation.definitionFit: Beauvais in northern France has a Gothic cathedral with the tallest choir ever built, so the town names the cathedral.

clue.text: Cocktail? Fix a soft drink before lawyer appears

parts.note: to pin is to fix in place
taken as written
cola is a fizzy soft drink
DA is a District Attorney, an American prosecutor

explanation.surface: Someone mixes a cocktail and then a soft drink before the lawyer turns up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' just orders the pieces: the DA comes after the drink. The question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A pina colada is a mixed drink of rum, coconut cream and pineapple juice, a well-known cocktail.

clue.text: Comic role in Shakespeare: slip up dropping one pole

indicators.note: dropping one means letting a single letter fall away from the word

parts.note: to slip up is to take a tumble
a staff is a long stick or pole

explanation.surface: An actor in a Shakespeare comedy role trips and drops a pole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' looks like an N or S, the usual crossword poles, but here it is the whole stick, and the letter dropped is from the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir John Falstaff is the fat, boastful knight of Henry IV and The Merry Wives of Windsor, Shakespeare's best-loved comic character.

clue.text: Hard time recalling forename of WWI heroine

indicators.note: recalling means calling back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: H is the pencil abbreviation for hard
tide is an old word for time or season, as in Yuletide

explanation.surface: Someone struggles to remember the first name of a First World War heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: H plus TIDE read backwards gives EDITH.
explanation.definitionFit: Edith Cavell was the British nurse executed in 1915 for helping Allied soldiers escape occupied Belgium, so her first name fits.

clue.text: Adolescent limped: he's gone over on uncovered toys

indicators.note: something that has gone over has been turned upside down, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: to hobble is to walk lamely
he turned over

indicators.note: uncovered means stripped of its outer layer, so only the inner letters stay

parts.note: the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A teenager hobbled about after falling over on toys left lying around.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the pieces in order below: HOBBLED, then EH, then OY from tOYs.
explanation.definitionFit: Hobbledehoy is an old word for a clumsy, awkward youth, a gangling teenager between boyhood and manhood.

clue.text: Leave with detective before finale — that's a bit of good fortune

parts.note: to go is to leave
DS is a Detective Sergeant
the finale is the end

explanation.surface: Getting time off with a police officer just before the climax counts as luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' and 'before' only set the order of the three pieces; a Detective Sergeant is a British police rank.
explanation.definitionFit: A godsend is an unexpected stroke of luck arriving just when needed, as if sent from heaven.

clue.text: Street resident finally turning up in street, possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals one arrangement among many, so the letters may be rearranged
finally points to the very end, so only the closing letter of the word is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word
taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: Someone living on the street is perhaps finally getting back on their feet there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning up' looks like a phrase meaning arriving, but 'turning' supplies its last letter while 'up in street' is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A guttersnipe is a scruffy child of the slums who lives largely on the streets, so a street dweller.

clue.text: Problem involving husband, bar, drunk — it generates conversation

indicators.note: to involve is to take in, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: the rub is the difficulty, as in 'there's the rub'
H is the abbreviation for husband

indicators.note: drunk means reeling and unsteady, so the letters stagger out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A husband and a drunken session at the bar are the cause of plenty of talk.
explanation.walkthrough: RUB takes in H to make RHUB; BAR rearranged adds ARB. Actors murmur 'rhubarb' repeatedly to fake background chatter.
explanation.definitionFit: On stage, extras repeating the word produce the noise of crowd talk, so it creates the sound of conversation.

clue.text: Recommend fruity drink when going round a part of Ireland

parts.note: to tip is to recommend, as a racing tip

indicators.note: going round means encircling, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: perry is an alcoholic drink made from pears
taken as written

explanation.surface: A travel suggestion: try the local fruit cider when touring an Irish county.
explanation.walkthrough: Perry is the pear equivalent of cider; it goes round A after TIP.
explanation.definitionFit: Tipperary is a county in the Irish province of Munster, famous from the wartime song.

clue.text: Rascals splitting least colourful historic document

indicators.note: something splitting another forces its way into the middle of it

parts.note: the palest thing has the least colour
imps are mischievous children

explanation.surface: Naughty children tear apart a faded old manuscript.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Least colourful' reads as describing the document, but it is the word being split open.
explanation.definitionFit: A palimpsest is an ancient manuscript scraped and reused, with earlier writing still faintly visible beneath the newer text.

clue.text: Everybody gathering around closed part of the Maldives

indicators.note: gathering around means crowding about something, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: all means everybody
a door pushed to is shut

explanation.surface: Everyone crowds round a resort in the Maldives that has shut.
explanation.walkthrough: Closed in the sense of a door pulled to is a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: The Maldives consist of coral atolls, ring-shaped reefs enclosing lagoons, so one atoll is a piece of the country.

clue.text: Arctic region — leader stricken with illness calling me in

indicators.note: calling someone in means summoning them inside, so one piece goes within another
something stricken is struck down and knocked about, so its letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material
taken as written, as anagram material
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sick expedition leader in the Arctic sends for help to be brought in.
explanation.walkthrough: LEADER and ILLNESS together are rearranged, then ME is called into the middle. 'Leader' wants to mean a first letter, but here it is fodder whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Ellesmere Island is the northernmost island of the Canadian Arctic archipelago, a huge frozen polar territory.

clue.text: No place for tit's wing in remarkable bird

indicators.note: having no place for something means leaving it out

parts.note: startling means striking or remarkable

indicators.note: a wing is a side part, so only the edge letter of the word is used

parts.note: the first letter of the small bird's name, its leading wing

explanation.surface: A notable bird has no room for a tit on its wing.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing a T from STARTLING leaves the bird. 'Tit' tempts you to look for a bird in the wordplay, but only its edge letter is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: The starling is a common songbird with glossy speckled plumage, famed for its huge swirling flocks.

clue.text: European piece of film on convulsive movement in part of the heavens

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for European
a clip is a short extract from a film
a tic is an involuntary twitch

explanation.surface: A European film clip shows a twitching motion somewhere in the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'on' sets CLIP above TIC.
explanation.definitionFit: The ecliptic is the apparent annual path of the sun across the celestial sphere, a great circle of the sky.

clue.text: Business graduate seen following beginnings of song and dance

indicators.note: beginnings are starts, so just the opening letters of the words are taken

parts.note: opening letters of each word
an MBA is a Master of Business Administration

explanation.surface: An MBA graduate is spotted joining in the singing and dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Song and dance' looks like one phrase, but 'dance' alone is the definition. MBA comes after the two initials.
explanation.definitionFit: The samba is a lively Brazilian ballroom and carnival dance of African origin.

clue.text: One might catch you saying it doesn't measure involuntary responses

definitions.text: One might catch you saying it doesn't measure involuntary responses

parts.words: One might catch you saying it doesn't measure involuntary responses
parts.note: surface reading: a gadget that would catch you out denying what it records
setter's reading: claiming it measures nothing is a lie, and this machine is built to catch liars

explanation.walkthrough: The machine records pulse, sweating and breathing, which are involuntary, so denying it does so would be a lie, exactly what it detects.
explanation.definitionFit: A polygraph is a lie detector, recording bodily reactions such as heart rate while a subject answers questions.

clue.text: Fetch up carrying old queen's wig

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it, so one piece holds another

parts.note: to fetch up is slang for to vomit
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the royal cipher

explanation.surface: Someone retrieves an elderly monarch's hairpiece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fetch up' looks like fetching something, but it is slang for being sick; the queen sits just after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A peruke is a long periwig of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the word from which periwig derives.

clue.text: Good connecting passage provided by a Russian composer

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good
a link connects two things
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fine transitional passage in a score was written by a Russian composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Connecting passage' sounds musical, fitting the surface, but it is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Mikhail Glinka wrote the opera A Life for the Tsar and is regarded as the father of Russian classical music.

clue.text: Preferring solitude in urinals when tipsy

indicators.note: a tipsy person staggers about, so the letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: A drunk man in a gents' toilet would rather be left alone.
explanation.walkthrough: The seven letters of URINALS rearrange to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Insular describes someone inward-looking and detached, keeping to themselves like an island cut off from others.

clue.text: Wages bringing in 14, say, in Scottish town

indicators.note: to bring something in is to take it inside, so one piece enters another

parts.note: pay means wages
the answer to 14, an atoll, is an example of an island

explanation.surface: Pay that brings in fourteen pounds or so in a Scottish town.
explanation.walkthrough: '14, say' points to the answer at 14, ATOLL; 'say' marks it as an example of an ISLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Paisley is a large town west of Glasgow, once a weaving centre that gave its name to the teardrop textile pattern.

clue.text: See 1
2 getting end away in German city

indicators.note: having the end sent away means the final letter is removed

parts.note: the answer to 2 down, a zealot

explanation.surface: A fanatic gets rid of an ending in a German city.
explanation.walkthrough: The 2 refers to the answer at 2 down, ESSENE; lose its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Essen is an industrial city in the Ruhr valley of western Germany, long known for the Krupp steelworks.

clue.text: The sound of thieves makes you cry in exasperation

indicators.note: the sound of a word is how it is heard, not how it is written

parts.note: to nick is British slang for to steal, so nickers are thieves

explanation.surface: Hearing burglars at work is enough to make anyone swear in frustration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knickers!' is a mild British exclamation of annoyance; knickers are also women's underpants.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang the word is shouted as a mild expletive, an exclamation of irritation or disbelief.
